title: Midnight Coffee in Batam
subtitle: Why the toughest race conditions aren't solved in code, but in the stillness between sips.
quote: The human mind was never meant to run at 100% CPU utilization without idling.
excerpt: Sometimes the hardest bugs to fix are the ones in our own minds. A casual reflection on untangling race conditions, overcoming burnout, and discovering peace through a warm cup of coffee under the Batam night sky.
body:
It was 01:15 AM when I finally closed my IDE.

The text cursor had been blinking on line 412 for three consecutive hours. It was a vicious, nondeterministic race condition—the kind that vanishes when you attach a debugger and only blows up in production when two asynchronous network calls collide within a five-microsecond margin. My temples throbbed, and my shoulders felt like coiled cables under tension.

I shut the laptop lid, grabbed a faded windbreaker, and stepped out into the Batam night.

The Salt Air and Harbour Lights

The tropical island air hit first—heavy, humid, and carrying the distinctive scent of low-tide salt water mingled with wet asphalt from an evening downpour. I walked toward an open-air kedai kopi near Harbour Bay. The streets of Batam at this hour have a peculiar stillness. The daytime roar of scooters and container trucks fades into the distant, rhythmic thrum of cargo ship diesels moving through the Singapore Strait.

The coffee stall was bathed in the warm glow of a solitary bare incandescent bulb. Behind the stainless-steel counter, the uncle—whose apron bore the earned stains of ten thousand brews—greeted me with a knowing nod.

"Mas Farrel. Lembur lagi di depan layar ya? Kopi O pekat, gula sedikit?"
"Iya, Om. Seduh yang panas."

He pulled the cloth sock filter high into the air, creating a dramatic dark cascade of piping-hot Robusta into a thick ceramic mug. When he slid the cup across the weathered marble table, a rich crown of caramel foam floated on top, sending curling wisps of steam into the humid sea breeze.

Singapore Across the Strait

I sat by the edge of the stone terrace. Just across the dark Malacca Strait—barely twenty kilometers away—the Singapore skyline was ablaze. Marina Bay, the towering gantry cranes of Tanjong Pagar port, and the endless constellation of anchored container ships glowed like red and emerald LEDs pinned against velvet black. From here, all that relentless global ambition looked quiet. It looked manageable.

I took the first sip. The bitterness struck first—bold, earthy, roasted dark over charcoal—followed by a clean cocoa finish and a sudden warmth blooming in my chest.

In software engineering, we fall into the dangerous trap of treating our own biology like an overclocked server blade. We benchmark our productivity in commits per day, measure value by uptime, and dread idle threads.

I pulled a worn pocket notebook from my jacket and unscrewed my pen. I sketched two timelines on the paper. And just like that, the bug revealed itself in three simple arrows. The error wasn't in the network library; it was in my fundamental assumption that State A would always precede State B.

Sometimes the most effective code you will ever write happens when your hands are nowhere near a keyboard. Sometimes the brain simply needs twenty minutes of Batam breeze, a warm cup of coffee, and permission to sit quietly in the dark.
